clue.text: Rock transport holds nothing but is more than half full

parts.note: the Rock is the familiar nickname of Gibraltar, shortened to Gib

indicators.note: the transport word grips the nothing letter inside itself

parts.note: a bus is a form of public transport
nought, written as the letter O

explanation.surface: A vehicle on Gibraltar carries no passengers yet somehow counts as more than half full.
explanation.walkthrough: 'holds' puts O inside BUS to make BOUS, after GIB. The definition describes the moon between half and full.
explanation.definitionFit: A gibbous moon shows more than a half disc of light but is not yet a full circle.

clue.text: Unexpected good fortune closing the Ring Cycle

definitions.meaning: a welcome stroke of luck arriving out of the blue
Wagner's Ring ends with Götterdämmerung, the twilight or end of the gods

explanation.definitionFit: A windfall seems heaven-sent; and Wagner's last Ring opera shows the gods' end.

clue.text: Othello turns up under the table hence direction to company

indicators.note: in a down answer the second piece sits below the first

parts.note: a board is a table, as in bed and board

indicators.note: in a down clue the Othello word is turned to read upwards

parts.note: Othello is Shakespeare's Moor of Venice

explanation.surface: Shakespeare's tragic hero pops up beneath a table, offering stage directions to the troupe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turns up' reverses MOOR to ROOM, and 'under' places it below BOARD. 'company' is a firm, not a theatre troupe; directors meet here.
explanation.definitionFit: A firm's directors meet in this room, so instructions to the business come from there.

clue.text: Scent of a European flower, say?

indicators.note: the river's name is spoken, giving a word that sounds the same

parts.note: a flower is something that flows, a river; the Oder runs along the German-Polish border

explanation.surface: Asking what perfume a continental bloom gives off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flower' means a river (it flows). The Oder and the answer are said alike in British English, with no final R sound.
explanation.definitionFit: An odour is a smell, a scent given off by something.

clue.text: Villain corrected by uncle's rod

indicators.note: corrected letters are put into a different order, setting them right

explanation.surface: A rogue is punished with his uncle's cane.
explanation.walkthrough: 'corrected' rearranges UNCLES and ROD together.
explanation.definitionFit: A scoundrel is a dishonest rogue, a wicked person.

clue.text: One of the precursors of royalty in conversation with a walrus

definitions.text: One of the precursors of royalty in conversation with a walrus

parts.words: One of the precursors of royalty in conversation with a walrus
parts.note: in Lewis Carroll's poem the Walrus talks 'of shoes and ships and sealing-wax: the item listed just before kings

explanation.surface: Someone in line before the throne chats with a walrus.
explanation.walkthrough: The poem is 'The Walrus and the Carpenter' in Through the Looking-Glass; royalty means kings, and the vegetable comes before them in the famous line.
explanation.definitionFit: The leafy vegetable is named just ahead of kings in the Walrus's list of topics.

clue.text: Many on this island giving us building material

indicators.note: putting C and ON on the front of the answer gives the building material, so removing them leaves the island

parts.note: concrete is a building material
C is the Roman numeral for 100, so 'many'
taken as written

explanation.surface: Lots of people on a Mediterranean island supply us with construction supplies.
explanation.walkthrough: C plus ON in front of the island's name makes CONCRETE; the clue is read as C + ON + the island giving the building material.
explanation.definitionFit: Crete is the largest Greek island, in the eastern Mediterranean.

clue.text: "God for Harry! England and Saint. George" for instance at Harfleur

definitions.text: "God for Harry! England and Saint. George" for instance at Harfleur

parts.words: "God for Harry! England and Saint. George" for instance at Harfleur
parts.note: the closing shout of King Henry's speech before the walls of Harfleur in Shakespeare's Henry V, rallying troops to charge

explanation.surface: Quoting Shakespeare's Henry V rallying his army at the siege of Harfleur.
explanation.walkthrough: Harfleur is the French port besieged in Henry V; the speech opens 'Once more unto the breach' and ends with this rallying shout.
explanation.definitionFit: A rallying shout before a charge is exactly what King Henry gives his soldiers here.

clue.text: One who reached man's estate in this year of grace? Last month

parts.note: AD, anno Domini, 'in the year of our Lord', a year of grace
ult., short for ultimo, means last month in old business letters

explanation.surface: Asking whether someone came of age this year, last month in fact.
explanation.walkthrough: ULT (ultimo) is old commercial shorthand for 'of last month'. 'man's estate' means manhood.
explanation.definitionFit: Reaching man's estate means coming to full grown manhood, being fully grown up.

clue.text: You 'sound far from genuine though the sound is pleasing

indicators.note: the first word is spoken, written as letters that say the same thing

parts.note: the word you, spoken aloud
phony means fake, the opposite of genuine

explanation.surface: Someone sounds insincere even though their voice is agreeable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sound' after 'You' makes it a homophone: EU is said like 'you'. PHONY is the American spelling of phoney.
explanation.definitionFit: Euphony is harmony of sound, a quality of being agreeable to the ear.

clue.text: Stern Athenian gives nothing to Jack, say, on return

indicators.note: the card word is read from right to left, coming back on itself

parts.note: a jack is one example of a playing card
nought, written as the letter O

explanation.surface: A severe citizen of Athens hands nothing back to a sailor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on return' turns CARD into DRAC, and 'gives nothing to' adds O at the end. Draco was the Athenian lawgiver whose laws were famously harsh.
explanation.definitionFit: Draco drew up Athens's first written law code, so harsh it gave us the word draconian.

clue.text: How to foil the, rougher-sounding opponent

definitions.text: How to foil the, rougher-sounding opponent

parts.words: How to foil the, rougher-sounding opponent
parts.note: in bridge to ruff is to play a trump; an opponent who ruffs is a 'ruffer', which sounds like 'rougher', and you beat that card by playing a higher trump over it

explanation.surface: Advice on defeating an adversary who seems coarser than you.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rougher-sounding' is a card pun: 'rougher' sounds like ruffer, a player who ruffs (trumps) a trick. You foil them by beating their trump with a bigger one.
explanation.definitionFit: Beating an opponent's trump card with a higher trump of your own wins the trick from a player who has ruffed.

clue.text: Suffering torture under cane

indicators.note: to torture words is to twist them out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone endures a painful caning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'torture' rearranges UNDER and CANE together.
explanation.definitionFit: Endurance is the bearing of pain or hardship, the act of putting up with it.

clue.text: Very drunk with no head for a game of chance

indicators.note: the drunk word loses its opening letter

parts.note: blotto is slang for completely drunk

explanation.surface: Someone too drunk to think straight plays a game of luck.
explanation.walkthrough: BLOTTO loses its first letter, B.
explanation.definitionFit: Lotto is a lottery-style game in which numbers are drawn at random.

clue.text: Many a back-door character of endless mystery

parts.note: D is the Roman numeral for 500, so 'many'

indicators.note: the door word is turned to read backwards

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A shady figure who comes in by the rear entrance in a never-solved mystery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns DOOR into ROOD, after D. Dickens died before finishing The Mystery of Edwin Drood, so its mystery has no ending.
explanation.definitionFit: Edwin Drood is the title figure of Dickens's last novel, left unfinished at his death and never resolved.

clue.text: One making a statement for Tennyson's lady in the depression

indicators.note: the lady goes inside the depression word

parts.note: a dent is a hollow, a small depression
Lady Clara Vere de Vere is the subject of a Tennyson poem

explanation.surface: Someone speaks up on behalf of a melancholy Tennyson heroine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts CLARA inside DENT. 'depression' looks like low spirits but is a physical hollow.
explanation.definitionFit: A declarant is a person who makes a formal declaration, especially in law.

clue.text: One's in order eating here, with Smith in the priest's house

indicators.note: the initials of Smith are placed inside the priest's house

parts.note: a rectory is the house of a rector, a parish priest
F E Smith, the barrister and politician Lord Birkenhead, known by his initials

explanation.surface: Someone in good standing dines with Mr Smith at the vicarage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts FE inside RECTORY, after RE. 'One's in order' means a monk or nun of a religious order, who eats in this hall.
explanation.definitionFit: A refectory is the dining hall of a monastery or convent, where members of the order take meals.

clue.text: Extremity. of a print-supplier

definitions.meaning: the very end point of something
what leaves the marks police take for identification

explanation.definitionFit: It is the end of a digit, and the ridged pad there leaves the marks taken for identification.

clue.text: Superficial way Belloc's Matilda got into trouble

definitions.meaning: lying on the surface, on top of something

definitions.text: way Belloc's Matilda got into trouble
definitions.meaning: in Hilaire Belloc's cautionary tale 'Matilda, Who told Lies, and was Burned to Death', she told too many lies

explanation.definitionFit: A top layer rests on the surface, and Matilda's downfall was telling fibs too much.

clue.text: Stop cooking mice in sage

indicators.note: the mixed letters go inside the sage's name

parts.note: Solon was the wise lawgiver of Athens, so a sage

indicators.note: cooking a dish changes its ingredients, so the letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: An order to stop frying mice in a herb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cooking' turns MICE into EMIC, and 'in' puts that inside SOLON. 'sage' looks like the herb but is a wise man; 'Stop' means a punctuation mark.
explanation.definitionFit: In old printing usage a stop is any punctuation mark, and this one marks a pause between full stop and comma.

clue.text: Pinch a bit

definitions.meaning: a simple jointed mouthpiece for a horse

explanation.definitionFit: To pinch is to filch or nick something, and a horse's mouthpiece with a single joint goes by the same name.

clue.text: Surrender some interest for example

definitions.meaning: to give way or hand over
the return earned by an investment, such as interest or dividends

explanation.definitionFit: To give in means to cede ground, and an investment's return in income is also called by this word.

clue.text: Resentment .when unexplored shell has gone astray

parts.note: a dud is a shell that fails to go off

indicators.note: letters gone astray wander out of place, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Bitterness when a bomb that never went off has been lost.
explanation.walkthrough: 'astray' rearranges GONE into GEON, after DUD. The newspaper text held here reads 'unexplored'; the page prints 'unexploded'.
explanation.definitionFit: Dudgeon is a feeling of offence or indignation, as in 'in high dudgeon'.

clue.text: Getting firsts 'in all college con-: - -tests ranks as capital

indicators.note: the opening letter of each of the following words is taken, as if each word gave up its first

explanation.surface: Top marks across every college competition rank one as a capital achievement.
explanation.walkthrough: The first letters of the five words after 'in' spell the answer, the capital of Ghana.
explanation.definitionFit: Accra is the capital city of Ghana in West Africa.

clue.text: Papal court is somewhat mercurial

indicators.note: only part of the following word is used, the run of letters sitting inside it

explanation.surface: The Vatican's governing body is said to be rather changeable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is somewhat' takes the letters inside MERCURIAL.
explanation.definitionFit: The Curia is the body of departments through which the Pope governs the Catholic Church.

clue.text: Rival has deep trouble: but won the day

indicators.note: letters in trouble are thrown into disorder and rearranged

explanation.surface: A competitor is in deep difficulty but still comes out on top.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trouble' rearranges RIVAL and DEEP together.
explanation.definitionFit: To prevail is to triumph or win through, as in carrying the day.

clue.text: Copper to go ahead and submit legal argument

parts.note: p, a penny, was a copper coin
to lead is to go in front

explanation.surface: A policeman goes first and presents his case in court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' suggests a policeman, but it is a copper coin, a penny, abbreviated P.
explanation.definitionFit: To plead is to argue a case or address a court on someone's behalf.

clue.text: Always a caution this girl of many amours

definitions.meaning: the middle traffic light always warns drivers to take care
the heroine of Kathleen Winsor's novel Forever ..., who has many lovers

explanation.definitionFit: The yellow traffic signal warns of a change, and the heroine of Kathleen Winsor's racy novel Forever Amber has many lovers.

clue.text: Immovable catkin? Heavens above!

parts.note: firm means fixed and unmoving
an ament is a botanical word for a catkin

explanation.surface: An exclamation of surprise at a catkin that will not budge.
explanation.walkthrough: AMENT is a botanist's word for a catkin. 'Heavens above!' reads as an exclamation but is the definition: the sky overhead.
explanation.definitionFit: The firmament is the vault of the sky, the heavens arching overhead.

clue.text: Bath victim of G J Smith could get well in a house of correction

definitions.text: Bath victim of G J Smith

indicators.note: the answer gets the word well added to become the prison word, so taking well away from the prison leaves the answer

parts.note: Bridewell was a London prison, and its name became a general word for a house of correction
taken as written

explanation.surface: A murdered newlywed might recover in a reformatory.
explanation.walkthrough: George Joseph Smith drowned his wives in the bath (the 'Brides in the Bath' murders, 1915). Add WELL to the answer and you get BRIDEWELL, an old word for a prison.
explanation.definitionFit: Smith's victims were women he had just married, each drowned in her bath.

clue.text: Played the part of a legislator?.

definitions.meaning: what a lawmaker does to a bill, making it law

explanation.definitionFit: An actor performs a role this way, and a parliament passes a measure into law the same way.

clue.text: Ideal type of quiet old' Spanish kingdom

parts.note: p is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly
Aragon was a medieval kingdom in north-east Spain

explanation.surface: The perfect specimen of a hushed old Spanish realm.
explanation.definitionFit: A paragon is a model of excellence, a perfect example of its kind.
